mappings.concept: Horizontally scaling a pool of identical machines
mappings.breaks_when: A Google managed instance group is created as either zonal or regional, and the regional form spreads instances across zones for you. An AWS Auto Scaling group achieves the same thing by being given subnets in several availability zones, because the subnet is what carries the zone. Note the acronym trap: AWS ASG means Auto Scaling group, while Azure ASG means application security group, an unrelated networking object.

Cloud Functions (2nd gen) is now Cloud Run functions and uses the Cloud Run service model. The first generation remains distinct. Azure Functions behavior depends on the hosting plan, including timeout, scaling, and cold starts. AWS Lambda has its own invocation and concurrency model. A familiar function name does not establish identical runtime limits; check the generation, trigger, and hosting plan.

mappings.concept: Running a container without managing servers
mappings.breaks_when: Fargate supplies compute for ECS or EKS, so an orchestrator remains part of the design. Azure Container Apps and Cloud Run expose a managed application deployment experience. Cloud Run services can scale to zero by default, but minimum instances and billing mode change idle behavior and cost. Storage, networking, databases, and other dependencies can still incur charges while application instances are at zero. Compare the whole architecture and the selected hosting plan.

Compare the operating mode, not just the Kubernetes service name. GKE Autopilot, EKS Auto Mode, and AKS Automatic all reduce infrastructure management, with different node controls, workload constraints, upgrade behavior, and billing. They are relevant alternatives, not identical products. GKE Autopilot billing can depend on workload and compute class; do not assume every workload is billed only by requested pod resources. Check the selected mode, region, and supported features.

mappings.concept: Deploy code, platform manages the runtime
mappings.breaks_when: The deployment and operating units differ. Azure App Service has deployment slots; Elastic Beanstalk manages visible AWS resources and supports blue/green deployment through environment URL swaps; App Engine supports versions and traffic allocation. These are related release patterns with different configuration, scaling, and rollback behavior. Compare the runtime, plan, and deployment unit rather than claiming that staging exists in only one cloud.

mappings.shared_trap: The concept transfers cleanly, and the naming history is the trap. Google's older preemptible VMs had a hard 24-hour maximum lifetime; Spot VMs do not, and material written before the change still teaches the 24-hour limit. All three remain unsuitable for anything that cannot tolerate reclamation at short notice.

azure.name: Azure SQL Database, or Azure Database for PostgreSQL and MySQL

mappings.breaks_when: Azure splits by engine into separate products, whereas RDS and Cloud SQL are one product with an engine choice. Azure SQL Database is also not simply hosted SQL Server: it is a platform service with its own feature set, distinct from Azure SQL Managed Instance, which is the closer match for lifting an existing SQL Server across. Picking between Database, Managed Instance and SQL on a VM is a recurring AZ-305 question.

mappings.concept: High availability versus read scaling on a relational database

aws.name: RDS Multi-AZ DB instance or DB cluster; read replica

mappings.breaks_when: In RDS, a Multi-AZ DB instance has a non-readable standby, while a Multi-AZ DB cluster has two readable standby instances that also support failover. Ordinary RDS read replicas are a separate asynchronous replication mechanism; do not infer automatic failover from readability. Azure SQL Database zone redundancy and read scale-out depend on service tier; active geo-replication is a separate readable asynchronous copy. Cloud SQL for MySQL regional HA uses a standby for failover; a read replica serves reads separately. Specify the engine, deployment type, and failure scope before choosing.

These products share some workloads but differ in data model and consistency controls. DynamoDB supports key-value and document data; Cosmos DB capabilities depend on the selected API. Firestore is document-oriented; Bigtable uses a wide-column model. Choose from required queries, transactions, consistency, throughput, and regional design, rather than translating a product name. A provider may offer several relevant database products beyond this shortlist.

azure.name: Microsoft Fabric Warehouse or Azure Synapse Analytics
azure.note: Separate products and operating models. Exam retirement does not establish service retirement.

mappings.breaks_when: Compare the actual deployment model: provisioned or serverless Redshift, Fabric Warehouse or Synapse SQL options, and BigQuery. Provisioned clusters and consumption-oriented services expose different capacity and cost controls. Fabric and Synapse are separate choices; retirement of an exam is not proof that a service is retired. Evaluate existing integrations, workload, governance, and purchasing model.

azure.name: Azure Managed Redis
azure.note: Azure Cache for Redis has a published retirement and migration schedule; consult the FAQ for tier-specific dates.

mappings.breaks_when: An in-memory cache is a shared concept, but engine/version support, persistence, clustering, failover, and networking depend on the product and tier. Microsoft is moving Azure Cache for Redis users to Azure Managed Redis on a published schedule. A new design should compare current offerings rather than treating an old cache name as a stable equivalent.

aws.name: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, and separately SNS and SQS

azure.name: Azure Event Hubs, and separately Service Bus and Event Grid

mappings.breaks_when: Queue processing, event routing, topic fan-out, and replayable streams are distinct requirements. AWS offers Kinesis, SQS, and SNS; Azure offers Event Hubs, Service Bus, and Event Grid; Google Pub/Sub overlaps several of these workloads. Compare ordering scope, acknowledgements, replay/retention, transactions, and delivery semantics for the chosen service. A queue requirement does not by itself select a streaming service.

An AWS account is simultaneously the isolation boundary, the billing boundary and the identity boundary. Azure and Google Cloud split those across three different objects: an Entra tenant holds identity, a subscription or billing account holds spend, and the subscription or project holds resources. Assuming one object does all three is the single most common cross-cloud modelling error.

mappings.concept: Grouping container above the isolation boundary
mappings.breaks_when: Nesting depth differs and is tested. AWS allows five levels of OUs below a root. Azure allows six levels of management groups, excluding the root and subscription levels, with 10,000 management groups per directory. Google allows ten levels of folders, with at most 300 direct child folders per parent. The Azure root management group cannot be moved or deleted, its ID equals the tenant ID, and Azure Resource Manager caches the hierarchy for up to 30 minutes so a move can appear not to have happened.

mappings.concept: Grouping container below the isolation boundary

aws.name: Resource group
aws.note: Optional resource grouping; deleting the group does not delete members.

azure.name: Resource group
azure.note: Lifecycle container for resources deployed at resource-group scope.

gcp.note: No equivalent. Labels and separate projects do this job.

mappings.breaks_when: An Azure resource group is a lifecycle and management scope for resources deployed at resource-group scope. Deleting the group initiates deletion of its contents, subject to locks, dependencies, and service behavior. An AWS Resource Group is a grouping/query construct; deleting that group does not delete its member resources. Google projects and labels provide different grouping boundaries. Not every Azure resource type is deployed at resource-group scope.

mappings.concept: Scope of the virtual network object
mappings.breaks_when: A Google VPC is a global object spanning every region and carries no CIDR of its own; the subnets hold the ranges and are regional. One Google VPC can contain instances in Tokyo and Frankfurt that route to each other over Google's backbone with no peering. AWS and Azure networks are regional, so the same design needs peering or a transit construct. An AWS subnet additionally lives in exactly one availability zone, whereas Azure and Google subnets are regional and span zones.

mappings.concept: Independent failure domain within a region
mappings.breaks_when: Azure additionally has an availability set, which is not a zone. An availability set uses fault domains and update domains inside a single datacentre and protects against rack failure and host patching, not against a datacentre outage. Any question naming a datacentre-level failure wants zones, and the availability set is a deliberate distractor. AWS also shuffles zone names per account, so us-east-1a in two accounts is generally not the same physical zone; the stable identifier is the AZ ID such as use1-az1.

An SCP sets a ceiling on what IAM may grant and never grants anything itself; if the SCP allows an action and no IAM policy grants it, the answer is still no. Azure Policy is a different kind of engine: it evaluates resource configuration at write time and can deny a deployment RBAC would have permitted, so it answers "is this configuration allowed" rather than "may this principal act". A maximum of ten SCPs attach to any root, OU or account, and when SCPs are enabled every entity must have at least one attached at all times.

These are different categories of object. An AWS role is an identity you assume, with its own temporary credentials issued by STS and a trust policy naming who may assume it. An Azure or Google role is a named set of permissions that carries no credentials and does nothing until assigned to a separate principal at a scope. The nearest AWS equivalent of an Azure or Google role is a managed policy; the nearest Azure or Google equivalent of an AWS role is a service principal or service account.

mappings.concept: Credentials for compute without stored secrets
mappings.breaks_when: Azure splits this into system-assigned, which is bound to one resource and deleted with it, and user-assigned, which is a standalone resource that survives and can be shared; "must outlive the VM" or "shared by several apps" selects user-assigned. AWS requires an instance profile as a wrapper around the role, which the console creates invisibly and which then appears unannounced in CLI questions. A Google service account is both an identity and a resource, so using one requires a role on the service account itself, typically Service Account User, separate from any permission the account holds.

mappings.concept: How a permission decision is reached

aws.name: IAM policy evaluation by request context

azure.name: Deny assignment, then additive union of role assignments

gcp.name: Deny policy, then additive union of allow policy bindings

mappings.breaks_when: AWS evaluates applicable grants and restrictions rather than requiring an allow at every stage of a universal pipeline. Identity-based grants are constrained by boundaries and applicable organization or session policies. Same-account resource-based grants can behave differently depending on whether they name a user, role, or role session; an applicable explicit deny still wins. Azure RBAC and Google IAM allow grants inherit down their resource hierarchies, but deny controls and conditions must also be considered. A narrower role at a child scope does not remove an inherited grant.

mappings.concept: Administering the directory versus administering resources

aws.name: IAM Identity Center administration and account IAM

azure.name: Microsoft Entra roles and Azure RBAC roles

gcp.name: Cloud Identity super administrator and organization IAM roles

mappings.breaks_when: Directory administration and workload access are different responsibilities in all three ecosystems. An Azure Global Administrator does not automatically receive resource permissions: elevation grants User Access Administrator at root scope, from which resource access can be assigned. Google Workspace or Cloud Identity super administrators manage the directory; Organization Administrator manages organization IAM and is not an unrestricted workload superuser. AWS Identity Center administration likewise does not replace the permission sets and IAM roles used to access member-account resources.

mappings.concept: Workforce single sign-on into the cloud

gcp.name: Cloud Identity, or Workforce Identity Federation

mappings.breaks_when: Entra ID is the identity system Azure is built on, so it is always present. AWS IAM Identity Center is an optional layer added on top of per-account IAM, and IAM users still exist underneath. Both were renamed recently enough that most third-party course material still says Azure AD and AWS SSO, which is what candidates will have been taught.

aws.name: Secrets Manager, or SSM Parameter Store

mappings.breaks_when: Azure Key Vault is one service holding secrets, keys and certificates, so it also occupies the slot that AWS gives to KMS and Google gives to Cloud KMS. AWS splits the job in two, and the split is tested: Secrets Manager rotates automatically and is billed per secret, while Parameter Store is cheaper, has a free standard tier and does not rotate on its own. "Automatic rotation" selects Secrets Manager.

An AWS security group has allow rules, not explicit deny rules. If broad allow rules must remain while one address is blocked, use an appropriate deny-capable control, such as a network ACL, network firewall, or application-layer control where applicable. Azure NSGs and Google VPC firewall rules support allow and deny decisions with priorities. Google VPC firewall rules belong to the network and select targets; do not assume all three attach and evaluate identically.

azure.note: An NSG on the subnet fills this position but is stateful.

gcp.note: VPC firewall rules are stateful; they do not reproduce the AWS network ACL model.

mappings.breaks_when: AWS network ACLs are stateless: allowing an inbound request does not automatically permit its outbound reply. Return traffic needs a matching rule. Azure NSGs and the Google VPC firewall rules compared here are stateful, so their connection tracking differs. This comparison concerns these native controls, not every possible firewall appliance or policy product.

mappings.concept: Reaching a managed service without traversing the internet

azure.name: Private endpoint, and separately service endpoint

gcp.name: Private Service Connect, and separately Private Google Access

mappings.breaks_when: Azure's service endpoint and private endpoint sound like synonyms and are not. A service endpoint keeps traffic on the Microsoft backbone while the service keeps its public IP and nothing enters your address space. A private endpoint puts a network interface with a private IP from your subnet in front of the service, so it becomes addressable inside the VNet and reachable from on-premises over ExpressRoute or VPN, which service endpoints cannot do. "Must be reachable from on-premises" or "must have a private IP" selects private endpoint. The AWS pair has the same shape: a gateway endpoint is a route table entry, is free, and serves only S3 and DynamoDB, while an interface endpoint is a real network interface, works for most services, and is billed hourly plus data.

aws.name: CloudFront, or Global Accelerator for layer 4

mappings.breaks_when: Google's global external Application Load Balancer uses a single anycast IP worldwide natively, so one address serves every region. AWS and Azure reach the same outcome by placing a separate global service in front of regional load balancers. Do not confuse Azure Front Door with Traffic Manager: Traffic Manager is DNS only, hands out an answer and then leaves the path, and therefore cannot terminate TLS, rewrite a header or fail over a live connection. Any question mentioning header-based routing or TLS offload at the edge is a Front Door question. Route 53 occupies the same DNS-only position in AWS.

mappings.shared_trap: Peering between A and B and between B and C does not by itself give A a transit path to C in any of these three services. Check address-range overlap and supported route types: peering products have provider-specific restrictions and exceptions. A transitive design requires a supported transit or routing solution, not a chain of ordinary peerings.

mappings.breaks_when: An AWS NAT gateway is a zonal resource, so a zone-resilient design needs one per zone and pays for each, which turns up as both a cost question and an availability question. Cloud NAT is a software-defined feature of the network rather than an appliance in the data path, so there is nothing to place in a subnet or size. The three are billed on different shapes, which matters in cost-optimisation scenarios.

Azure Blob Storage uses a container within a storage account; the account carries settings such as redundancy and naming. S3 and Cloud Storage expose buckets. An Azure blob container is unrelated to the container image used to package an application. Google bucket location options include regional, dual-region, and multi-region; compare these with replication and redundancy configurations in the other providers rather than assuming identical placement controls.

Retrieval behaviour differs fundamentally and decides questions. Google's Archive class is online: it has the same millisecond first-byte latency as Standard and you simply pay more to read it, with a 365-day minimum storage duration. AWS Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive are offline and need a restore job taking minutes to hours. The Azure Archive tier is also offline and needs rehydration, which can take hours. So "archive but must be readable instantly" is achievable natively on Google, needs Glacier Instant Retrieval on AWS, and is not the Archive tier on Azure. Minimum durations also differ, and early deletion is charged as if the object had been kept for the minimum.

mappings.concept: Network-attached block storage for a VM
mappings.breaks_when: Google Persistent Disk can be created as regional, replicating synchronously across two zones in a region, which EBS cannot do; EBS volumes are strictly zonal and cross-zone resilience is a snapshot-and-restore or replication-at-the-application-layer problem. Google disks can also be resized and attached read-only to many instances at once, which changes what architectures are available.

Protocol support differs and is the deciding factor. Azure Files serves SMB and NFS, so it is the natural answer for Windows workloads and can be mounted directly from on-premises. EFS is NFS only, and Windows or Lustre workloads go to the separate FSx family. Filestore is NFS only.

mappings.concept: Naming the replication and durability setting

aws.name: Storage class, with zonal scope implied by the class

gcp.name: Location type, region, dual-region or multi-region

mappings.breaks_when: Azure configures redundancy on the storage account: LRS is local, ZRS spans zones, and geo-redundant options add asynchronous replication to a second region. Read-access variants expose the secondary. S3 storage classes include both One Zone-IA and Express One Zone as single-zone choices; other classes have different resilience and retrieval characteristics. Google Cloud Storage separates location type from storage class. Choose resilience and access behavior independently where the platform allows it.

aws.meaning: An assumable identity with its own temporary credentials issued by STS, and a trust policy naming who may assume it.

azure.meaning: A named set of permissions, meaningless until assigned to a separate principal at a scope.

gcp.meaning: A named collection of permissions, bound to a member at a resource node.

terms.why_it_hurts: An AWS role is a thing you become; the other two are lists of verbs pinned to somebody else. Different categories of object behind one word. The nearest AWS equivalent of an Azure or Google role is a managed policy, and the nearest Azure or Google equivalent of an AWS role is a service principal or service account.

aws.meaning: An optional, tag-driven query that produces a view over resources. It owns nothing.

azure.meaning: A mandatory lifecycle container. Every resource is in exactly one, and deleting the group deletes everything inside.

terms.why_it_hurts: Identical phrase, unrelated concepts, and one of them is destructive. Deleting an Azure resource group destroys every resource in it without a per-resource prompt. Deleting an AWS resource group destroys nothing. Google has no construct at this level at all.

aws.meaning: A JSON document listing actions, resources and conditions, attached to an identity or a resource.

azure.meaning: Azure Policy is a governance engine evaluating resource configuration at write time. It is not the permissions system.

gcp.meaning: Either an IAM allow policy, which is a list of role bindings, or an organization policy, which is a configuration constraint.

terms.why_it_hurts: In AWS, policy is how permissions work. In Azure, permissions are RBAC and Azure Policy is a separate system answering a different question. A scenario about enforcing a required configuration is an Azure Policy answer and every RBAC option is a distractor. Google uses the word for both of its systems, so context decides.

aws.meaning: Auto Scaling group. A pool of identical instances scaled by policy.

azure.meaning: Application security group. A named group of network interfaces that NSG rules can reference instead of listing addresses.

terms.why_it_hurts: One acronym, two services, different domains entirely, and both are common enough that the abbreviation gets used unqualified in study notes and team chat. Expand it every time.

aws.meaning: An OCI container image or running container. The storage equivalent is a bucket.

azure.meaning: In Blob Storage, a grouping of blobs inside a storage account. Roughly what the other clouds call a bucket.

gcp.meaning: An OCI container image or running container. The storage equivalent is a bucket.

terms.why_it_hurts: Azure uses the word for both meanings in the same portal. "Create a container" in a storage context means a blob grouping and has nothing to do with Docker, Kubernetes or Container Apps. Reading it as a compute object sends the whole answer wrong.

aws.meaning: No such construct. Spreading across datacentres means using several Availability Zones, and placement groups solve a different problem.

azure.meaning: A grouping using fault domains and update domains inside a single datacentre, protecting against rack failure and host patching.

gcp.meaning: No such construct. Spread placement policies exist for physical separation, but the failure domain you design against is the zone.

terms.why_it_hurts: It sounds like an availability zone and is not one. An availability set does not protect against a datacentre outage; an availability zone does. AWS and Google have no equivalent construct, so there is nothing to translate it to. Any question naming a datacentre-level failure wants zones, and the availability set is a deliberately placed wrong answer.

aws.meaning: A VPC endpoint. Gateway endpoints are free route table entries serving only S3 and DynamoDB; interface endpoints are billed network interfaces serving most services.

azure.meaning: Two unrelated things. A service endpoint keeps traffic on the backbone while the service keeps its public IP. A private endpoint puts a private IP from your subnet in front of the service.

gcp.meaning: Private Service Connect endpoints, plus Private Google Access as a separate subnet setting.

terms.why_it_hurts: The Azure pair is the worst naming collision in cloud networking. Service endpoint and private endpoint sound like synonyms and behave differently: only the private endpoint gives the service an address inside your network and only it works from on-premises over ExpressRoute or VPN.

aws.meaning: Not a platform concept. The equivalent boundary is an account.

azure.meaning: Not a platform concept. The equivalent boundary is a subscription, or a resource group for lifecycle.

gcp.meaning: The mandatory container for all resources, with an immutable ID that can never be reused, plus a mutable name and an assigned number.

terms.why_it_hurts: Google projects are created far more freely than AWS accounts or Azure subscriptions, so the same word invites the wrong sense of weight. The ID, name and number are three different fields and questions exploit the difference; the ID is permanent and is not reusable even after the project is deleted.

aws.meaning: The isolation, billing and identity boundary all at once. Identified by a 12-digit number.

azure.meaning: Usually means a sign-in identity. A storage account is something else entirely, and a billing account something else again.

gcp.meaning: Usually a user identity. A billing account is a separate payable object linked to projects. A service account is a machine identity.

terms.why_it_hurts: Only in AWS does "the account" name the thing workloads live in. Saying "put it in another account" is a clear instruction on AWS and an ambiguous one everywhere else. Azure's storage account is a resource, not an identity, despite the name.

aws.meaning: A stateful allow-only filter attached to a network interface. It cannot deny.

azure.meaning: Network security group, a stateful filter with allow and deny rules evaluated by priority, attachable to a subnet, a NIC, or both.

gcp.meaning: No object by this name. VPC firewall rules do the job, attached to the network and targeted by tag or service account.

terms.why_it_hurts: The AWS object cannot deny anything, which people consistently forget, and Azure's similarly named object can. In Entra ID, "security group" additionally means a directory group of users, a third unrelated sense.

aws.meaning: A key-value label for billing, search and access control conditions.

azure.meaning: A key-value label for billing and search, usable as a condition in Azure Policy.

gcp.meaning: Two different things. Labels are key-value metadata for billing. Network tags are strings that select firewall rule targets and affect routing. Tags proper are a third, IAM-governed construct.

terms.why_it_hurts: A Google network tag is not metadata; it changes traffic behaviour by selecting which firewall rules apply. Treating it as a cosmetic label is how people accidentally expose or isolate an instance.

aws.meaning: Availability Zone, one or more discrete datacentres with independent power and cooling. Names are shuffled per account.

azure.meaning: Availability zone, the same idea, but not present in every region and opted into per resource.

gcp.meaning: A deployment area within a region, named like us-central1-a.

terms.why_it_hurts: Broadly the same concept, with two traps. AWS shuffles zone names per account, so us-east-1a is not the same physical place in two accounts; use the AZ ID such as use1-az1 when physical identity matters. Azure zones are not available in every region. The word also means a DNS zone in all three clouds.

aws.meaning: Not the term used. The equivalent is an IAM role assumed by a service.

azure.meaning: Not the term used. The equivalent is a service principal, or a managed identity that wraps one.

gcp.meaning: A machine identity that is simultaneously an identity and a resource. You grant it roles, and you grant others roles on it.

terms.why_it_hurts: The dual nature is the part candidates report failing. Using a Google service account requires a role on the service account itself, typically Service Account User, which is entirely separate from whatever permissions that service account holds.

aws.meaning: Amazon Machine Image, an AMI. Regional, and must be copied to be used in another region.

azure.meaning: A managed image, or a version published in an Azure Compute Gallery for replication and versioning.

gcp.meaning: A custom image, which is a global resource usable from any region without copying.

terms.why_it_hurts: Scope differs. Google images are global; AMIs are regional and need explicit copying, which is a step people forget in multi-region designs and which exam questions test directly.

aws.meaning: A CloudFormation stack, the set of resources created and deleted together from one template.

azure.meaning: A deployment, from an ARM template or Bicep file. Azure Stack is an unrelated hybrid hardware product.

gcp.meaning: A deployment, or a Terraform state in practice.

terms.why_it_hurts: Azure Stack is a distinct product line for on-premises hardware and has nothing to do with template deployments, so the word points at very different things depending on context.

aws.meaning: A billing commitment for capacity. Savings Plans are the newer, more flexible commitment.

azure.meaning: A reservation, purchased for one or three years.

gcp.meaning: A committed use discount. Google also applies automatic sustained use discounts with no commitment, which the other two do not have.

terms.why_it_hurts: Google's sustained use discount applies automatically for running an instance a large part of the month, with nothing purchased. There is no AWS or Azure equivalent, and it is a free mark on Cloud Digital Leader and Associate Cloud Engineer.
